title: What do 4 million students' responses tell us about mathematical understanding?
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton shares favourite findings from analysing over four million student responses to 12,000 diagnostic questions, each tagged with a construct and with every wrong answer mapped to the misconception it reveals. He reports that some misconceptions, like confusing squaring with doubling, fade with age while others, like swapping x and y coordinates, grow. Misconception prevalence is essentially identical for free-school-meal and other students and for girls and boys, which he reads as a case against differentiating instruction on those grounds. He also shows how one misconception, such as subtracting the smaller number from the larger, recurs across many constructs, and how machine-learned cascade diagrams link misconceptions causally. The piece is data-driven and implies curriculum sequencing should target root misconceptions early.
points: Each distractor is tagged with a specific misconception, so wrong answers become diagnostic data rather than noise.
Misconception trajectories differ: some decline with age, while mixing up x and y values increases, possibly because it is treated as assumed knowledge.
Misconception rates are tightly matched across income groups and genders, undermining differentiation along those lines.
The same misconception (subtracting smaller from larger) appears across mental subtraction, formal algorithms, decimals and standard form, so unaddressed early errors compound.
Cascade diagrams suggest root-cause misconceptions, with implications for curriculum ordering.
quotes: We selected 12,000 of our best diagnostic questions, tagged each with a construct, and mapped the 36,000 distractors to the associated misconceptions. We then collected over 4 million student responses and analysed the data.

Mixes up squaring and multiplying by 2 is an example of a misconception that remains prevalent across high school, but falls with age. It seems to be one of those things that requires regular exposure over time.

Whereas Mixes up the x and y values on the coordinates actually increases in prevalence as students get older! Is this because we don’t explicitly teach it past a certain age and treat it as assumed knowledge in more complex concepts older students encounter?
The answer is: no. The misconceptions are clustered tightly around the dashed line, indicating an equal prevalence for both groups of students.

This is good news. It means we don’t need to differentiate our instruction on any of these grounds, and instead can concentrate our efforts on delivering a high-quality learning experience for all our students.

We are particularly interested in how misconceptions relate to each other. Does a misconception in one area lead to misconceptions in other areas? Knowing this can help us identify the root causes of issues, which also has implications for curriculum ordering.
